summary: The Integration health page shows what an integration team monitors for the NovaBank connection: connection status, latency percentiles, error rate, request volume and ingest throughput. It loads `GET /integration/health` (status, versions and the self-describing endpoint catalog) and polls `GET /integration/metrics` every 4 seconds; because that endpoint returns only a current snapshot, the page keeps its own history to draw the trend lines. It also includes an API console that sends real requests through the low-level `request` helper and can copy any call as a cURL command.

notes.text: Header comment listing the page's four parts: connection status, service-level indicators (SLIs), a live API console and the endpoint catalog.
Besides `get`, imports `request`, the low-level call that never throws on HTTP errors and also returns the status, latency and request ID. That is exactly what the console needs.
DOM helpers and motion; `countUp` animates each metric from its previous value to the new one.
`microBars` (a tiny bar chart) and `sparkline` for the metric tiles; `jsonBlock` pretty-prints and colours JSON responses; `panel` frames each section.
`icon` and `toast`.
A ready-made `POST /events` body: a failed login from Lagos with four failed attempts from a suspicious IP. It is designed to trip several rules, so sending it returns a clearly elevated score.

`metric(key, label, unit)` renders one small SLI tile spanning 2 of the 12 columns: a label, a number that starts at `0`, an optional unit and an empty slot for its sparkline. `data-metric` lets `setMetrics` find each tile.
Page module titled `Integration`. It uses `ctx` for two intervals and one live subscription.
Loads connection health and the first metrics snapshot in parallel.

Client-side history for the trend lines. The metrics API reports only current values, so the page records each 4-second poll itself; the sparklines therefore start when the page opens and fill in over time.
Uptime seeded from the server, then advanced locally once a second, so the clock ticks without a request every second.

The endpoint catalog minus the SSE `/stream` route (a stream can't be shown in a request/response console), grouped by OpenAPI tag. `||=` creates each tag's array the first time the tag appears, and the comma operator returns `acc` from the reducer.
Mounts the page markup.
Header with a link to the auto-generated OpenAPI docs at `/docs`. It opens in a new tab, and `rel=noopener` stops that tab from reaching back into this page through `window.opener`.
Full-width **Connection** panel: a glowing status orb, the client and integration names, then `Connected` or `Degraded` with the API health beside it.
Fact row: uptime (`data-uptime`, ticks every second), API version, total events received (`data-received`, bumped by live events) and how long ago the last event arrived.

Which explanation engine the AI analyst uses (`openai` with its model, or `deterministic`), the rate limit, and how many dashboards are connected to the live stream (`data-clients`). The last line closes the panel.
The SLI row: six tiles for request count, the p50, p95 and p99 latency percentiles in ms, the error rate in %, and events ingested over the last 30 minutes.
Third row. The **API console** panel (7 columns) has a `Copy as cURL` button in its header.
The console's request bar: an HTTP method picker (POST selected by default), a path input relative to `/api/v1` (starting at `/events`) and a Send button.
The JSON body textarea, prefilled with `SAMPLE` and with spellcheck off, a meta line explaining that write calls carry the API key, and an empty response area. The last line closes the console.
**Endpoint catalog** panel (5 columns) with a route count, rendered as one heading per tag.

Each endpoint is a row whose `data-endpoint` holds the method and path separated by a space. It shows a coloured method badge, the path without `/api/v1`, its OpenAPI summary and a lock icon when the API key is required. The last line closes the row of panels.
Full-width **Busiest routes** panel, filled in by `setMetrics`.
`setMetrics(m, first)` applies one metrics snapshot to the page; `first` is true only for the initial call.
Picks the six tile values: total requests, the three latency percentiles, the error rate converted to a percentage, and ingest as the sum of the last 30 one-minute buckets.
Loops over the tiles. Latency and error rate show one decimal place; counts show whole numbers.
Animates each tile from its current value to the new one, taking 1.1 s on the first load and 0.6 s on later polls, with a formatter that keeps the decimal places steady while the number moves.
The ingest tile gets bars instead of a line: one bar per minute for the last 30 minutes, taken straight from the server's `throughput_per_minute`.
Appends each value to its client-side history and drops the oldest sample beyond 40 (about 2.7 minutes at one poll every 4 s), so memory use stays bounded.

From the second sample on, redraws the tile's sparkline: red for errors, neutral for requests, accent for latency. `animateIn: false` because the line is redrawn every 4 seconds, and replaying the draw-in animation each time would flicker.

Re-renders the **Busiest routes** table: route, call count, average latency and the number of 4xx/5xx responses (faded when zero). The server normalises IDs in routes, so `/users/USR-1001` is counted as `/users/{USR}`.
Updates the connected-dashboards count, then closes `setMetrics`.
Applies the first metrics snapshot with the longer count-up animation. The tiles themselves fade in with the router's page entrance, which staggers every grid child.
A local one-second tick for the uptime display. `ctx.every` stops it automatically when the user leaves the page.
Polls the metrics every 4 seconds. Each poll is itself an API call, so while this page is open the request count rises by at least one per poll: the page measures itself.
The console section starts with references to the method, path and body controls.
Delegated click: only clicks on a catalog row continue.
Splits the row's `data-endpoint` into method and path, and selects that method.
Strips the `/api/v1` prefix and swaps path parameters for real demo IDs (`EVT-00001`, `INC-0001`, `USR-1001`, `brute_force`), so the request is ready to send.
Prefills a sensible body: none for GET, the sample event for `/events`, a status change for incidents, a question for `/ask`, a signal list for `/evaluate`, and `{}` for anything else.
Briefly fades the body box (opacity 0.4 to 1) so the user notices it changed. The last line closes the listener.
The Send button handler. `meta` is the status line and `out` the response area.
For non-GET requests with a body, the JSON is parsed first; invalid JSON stops the send with a toast instead of sending a broken request.
Shows a shimmering line such as `Sending POST /events…` while waiting.
Sends the call with `request`, which adds the `X-API-Key` header for write methods and resolves even for 4xx/5xx responses, so errors are displayed rather than thrown.

The meta line: the status code styled as success or failure, round-trip time measured in the browser, the server's own processing time (`X-Response-Time`) and the `X-Request-ID`, which also appears in the server log, so a call can be traced end to end.
Renders the response body as syntax-coloured JSON and fades it in.
`request` throws only when no response arrives at all (for example when the server is down); that case shows `ERR` with the message. The last line closes the handler.
`Copy as cURL` builds an equivalent shell command. Write methods get an API-key header that references the `$IIP_API_KEY` environment variable, so the real key is never copied to the clipboard.
Adds the JSON body (whitespace collapsed to keep it on one line, wrapped in single quotes) and assembles the full command using this server's origin.
Copies the command with the async Clipboard API and shows a preview toast cut at 90 characters, or reports that clipboard access was blocked. The last line closes the handler.
Each `live:event` adds one to the **Events received** figure: commas are stripped from the formatted text before parsing, and `if (el)` is a defensive guard.
Closes `render` and the page object.
